parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation
parent.overview: 1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 is a crossroads, not one system: White develops the b1-knight before committing the c-pawn, which blocks White's own c-pawn and so gives up the usual c4 challenge to d5. The usual continuation is 2...Nf6, after which White chooses between 3.Bg5 (Richter-Veresov: pin on f6, queenside castling, f3 and e4) and 3.Bf4 (Jobava London: Nb5 ideas against c7, Qd2 and Bh6 against a fianchetto), or 3.Nf3 and transpositions. Other Black replies are 2...Bf5 (Alburt Defence, assessed as equal, rare in master play), 2...c5 (Irish Gambit, little explored) and 2...e6. The openings are rarely used by top players as a main weapon but are sound; Spassky, Tal, Karpov, Bronstein, Morozevich, Aronian and Gashimov have played them as surprise weapons. The subtree also swallows a different opening by transposition: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nc6 is the Chigorin Defence, Black's choice, not White's.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation
parent.overview: This root is the King's Indian reached by the move order 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.c4 (the same position as 3.Nf3 in the 2.c4 move order). It is not a distinct opening: it is the ordinary King's Indian, where Black fianchettoes with ...Bg7, castles, and strikes at White's centre with ...e5, ...c5 or ...f5. White's choice of set-up decides the character: the classical 4.Nc3 and e4 leads to the locked-centre opposite-wing race (c4-c5 against ...f5-f4), while the Fianchetto Variation (g3, Bg2, O-O, Nc3) is quieter, positional, and has less forcing theory. The data subtree groups 4.e4 Normal Variation lines (the majority of games) under this root, so it mixes both. Black's success depends on timing and coordination rather than automatic aggression.

parent.name: Bishop's Opening
parent.overview: White develops the bishop to c4 at once, eyeing f7 and discouraging ...d5, while keeping the f-pawn free for f4 and delaying the knight on g1. Unlike the Italian, White does not commit a knight to f3 on move two, so the opening is highly transpositional: after 2...Nc6 it tends to become an Italian or Vienna, after 2...Nf6 White usually plays 3.d3 (or the sharp Urusov Gambit 3.d4), and after 2...Bc5 play is symmetrical and can reach a Giuoco Piano. Theory judges it equal with best play. At master level it is a surprise weapon used to avoid Petrov preparation, not a main line.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 c6 2. d4 d5 3. Nc3 dxe4
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.e4 with ...c5 to trade a flank pawn for White's d-pawn, which leaves Black a central pawn majority and a half-open c-file in return for White's lead in development and space. This asymmetry is the point: Black plays for a win rather than equality. The usual pattern is White attacking on the kingside while Black counterattacks on the queenside along the c-file (...b5, ...Rc8), often with opposite-side castling in the sharpest lines. The root is a crossroads: after 2.Nf3 (about 80% of master games, s1) it branches into Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen, Classical, Sveshnikov, Taimanov and Kan, which range from forcing and theory-heavy (Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov) to flexible and solid (Kan, Classical, Taimanov). White's anti-Sicilians (Alapin, Closed, Grand Prix, 2.d3) avoid the Open Sicilian and are quieter. The root as a whole is the most played and most analysed opening at club and master level (s1).
